added: #Research the licensing requirements in your state. To find licensing requirements in your state, visit The American Society of Home Inspectors website. Licensing requirements vary from state to state and can range from no experience to a high school degree, coursework, licensure, and an apprenticeship. Find the requirements for your particular state so that you have an idea of what you'll need before you can get started.<ref>http://www.theashischool.com/Home-Inspection-Classes/Requirements-by-State</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Learn how houses are constructed. Having knowledge about electrical wiring, plumbing, heating systems, cooling systems, and roofing is critical if you want to be a good home inspector. Construction practices have changed over time, so a house that was built decades ago will be very different to one built recently. Having detailed knowledge about how all houses are constructed will give you a better understanding of dangerous housing conditions.<ref>http://inspectapedia.com/home_inspection/Become_A_Home_Inspector.php</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Take home inspection and licensing courses. There are various organizations and educational institutions that offer home inspection courses. If you don't want to go to a physical location like a Kaplan University, you can take online courses to achieve your license. Organizations that offer online courses include Inspection Certification Associates, American Home Inspectors Training, and the American Society of Home Inspectors.<ref>http://www.ahit.com/classes.htm</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Study for the home inspection exam. The National Home Inspector Examination (NHIE) offers a comprehensive list of content that will show up on your exam. Go to their website to get a copy of the outline and research each of the tops in greater detail. Make sure to study the content that will be on the test sufficiently before registering for the test.<ref>http://homeinspectionexam.org/prepare-for-the-exam/</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Register for the National Home Inspector Examination. The NHIE is required if you want to practice in 29 states including places like California, New York, Florida, and Texas. Register for the exam by visiting homeinspectionexam.org.<ref>http://homeinspectionexam.org/test-policies/</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Pass the home inspection exam and become certified. Once you've registered for the exam online, you'll likely be given a physical location and date that you'll have to take the test. Make sure to get plenty of rest the night before the test and study leading up to it.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 6 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Get a job at an established inspecting firm. Look on search engines and job boards for home inspecting job opportunities. Once you have the required certification and education, and have shadowed another home inspector, apply for the job. Companies are looking for clean-cut, organized, and dependable people. Follow the guidelines for a [[Have-a-Good-Job-Interview|good interview]] and be sure to communicate effectively and show up on time.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 7 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#[[Start-Your-Own-Business|Start your own business]]. If you don't want to work at a firm and already have some experience under your belt, you can start your own business. Home inspection businesses don't have a lot of need for human capital if you're the only one that will inspect the homes. To start your own home inspection company, you'll need a reliable vehicle, a computer and a minimum of $25,000 in working capital for overhead items.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 8 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Purchase a home inspecting franchise. A home inspection franchise will give you the initial tools and contacts that are required to land clients and start making money. Marketing and advertising is also usually covered in the form of logos and other promotional materials. Also, they will have methods that have been proven to be profitable in the past, as well as additional support if you're unsure what to do as a business owner. While the cost of a franchise can sometimes be costly, it may be worth the cost if you have limited experience.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 9 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Join a home inspectors organization. A home inspectors group will provide you a wealth of knowledge in the form of distance education and classroom training. The top organizations for home inspectors in the U.S. include the NAHI (The National Association of Home Inspectors) and the ASHI (The American Society of Home Inspectors). Both of these organizations have a significant number of members who work professionally as home inspectors. In addition to the education, you'll also be able to attend chapter meetings and workshops to talk about inspection and regulation.<ref>http://www.homeinspector.org/Become-a-home-inspector</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 10 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Get a mentor when first starting off. Some states require you dedicate hours towards an apprenticeship before you can become a certified home inspector. Even if your state doesn't require this, shadowing and working under a seasoned home inspector will give you insight and skills on how you should inspect homes. If you're part of a home inspector association, talk to veteran inspectors and ask if you can be an apprentice under them. If you aren't in an organization contact different firms and see if there is anyone available to take you under their wing.<ref>http://www.jobmonkey.com/howto/home-inspector/</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 11 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Go for additional training and education once you're an inspector. Look for regional meetings and seminars that you can attend to stay current and accurate. Many chapters of home inspection organizations will often put on educational events and workshops for existing inspectors.<ref>http://www.homeinspector.org/Calendar</ref> Also, you can use the time around your peers to network with other inspectors.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 12 Version 2.jpg|center]]

added: A home inspector is a person who comes and examines your home to see if it's up to code and if there is anything wrong with your house that must be repaired. Home inspectors make on average $57,340 per year and are a critical part of making sure that new and old construction is safe for people living or working around a building or home. Becoming a home inspector can be a fulfilling career that will require you to travel and interact with other people on a daily basis. By getting the right education and certification and continuing to hone your skills, you can get and keep your job as a home inspector.
==Steps==
===Getting Licenced===

#Research the licensing requirements in your state. To find licensing requirements in your state, visit The American Society of Home Inspector's website. Licensing requirements vary from state to state and can range from no experience to a high school degree, coursework, licensure, and an apprenticeship. Find the requirements for your particular state so that you have an idea of what you'll need before you can get started.<ref>http://www.theashischool.com/Home-Inspection-Classes/Requirements-by-State</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 4.jpg|center]]
#*Some states require you to also pass a background and criminal history check.<ref>https://www.ahit.com/news/tips-on-becoming-home-inspector.htm</ref>
#*In Texas you need to pass pre-licencing courses and complete 128 classroom hours before you can take your inspector's exam.
#*In New York you need to pass pre-licencing courses and complete 140 classroom hours.
#*Idaho does not require you to have a license to be a home inspector.<ref>http://fitsmallbusiness.com/how-to-become-a-home-inspector/</ref>

#Learn how houses are constructed. Having knowledge about electrical wiring, plumbing, heating systems, cooling systems, and roofing is critical if you want to be a good home inspector. Another thing to keep in mind is that houses are built during all time periods, and a house that was built decades ago will be very different to one built recently. Having detailed knowledge how all houses are constructed will give you a better understanding of dangerous housing conditions.<ref>http://inspectapedia.com/home_inspection/Become_A_Home_Inspector.php</ref>

#Take home inspection and licensing courses. There are various organizations and educational institutions that offer home inspection courses. If you don't want to go to a physical location like a Kaplan University, you can take online courses to achieve your license. Organizations that offer online courses include Inspection Certification Associates, American Home Inspectors Training, and the American Society of Home Inspectors.<ref>http://www.ahit.com/classes.htm</ref>

#Study for the home inspection exam. The National Home Inspector Examination (NHIE) offers a comprehensive list of content that will show up on your exam. Go to their website to get a copy of the outline and research each of the tops in greater detail. Make sure to study the content that will be on the test sufficiently before registering for the test.<ref>http://homeinspectionexam.org/prepare-for-the-exam/</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 5.jpg|center]]
#*Questions on the NHIE cover safety topics including, roof drainage, exterior doors and windows, driveways, landscaping, balconies, support structures, wiring and electrical, and plumbing.
#*The test is four hours long and has around 200 questions.

#Register for the National Home Inspector Examination. The NHIE is required if you want to practice in 29 states including places like California, New York, Florida, and Texas. Register for the exam by visiting homeinspectionexam.org.<ref>http://homeinspectionexam.org/test-policies/</ref>
#*Remember to check if this license is required in your state before paying for it.
#*In most state the exam costs $225.

#Pass the home inspection exam and become certified. Once you've registered for the exam online, you'll likely be given a physical location and date that you'll have to take the test. Make sure to get plenty of rest the night before the test and study leading up to it.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 6.jpg|center]]
#*If you fail your initial exam, you can retake the exam in 30 days if you pay another fee.
===Getting a Job===

#Get a job at an established inspecting firm. Look on online search engines and job boards for home inspecting job opportunities. Once you have the required certification, education, and have shadowed another home inspector, apply for the job. Companies are looking for clean-cut, organized, and dependable people. Follow the guidelines for a [[Have-a-Good-Job-Interview|good interview]] and be sure to communicate effectively and show up on time.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 12.jpg|center]]
#*You can also use any available networking connections and ask around to see which companies are looking for new employees.
#*When on the interview remember to emphasize your construction, regulation, and inspection knowledge.
#*A drawback from working for a firm is that they will typically take a 40-60% cut of your inspection fee.<ref>http://fitsmallbusiness.com/how-to-become-a-home-inspector/</ref>

#[[Start-Your-Own-Business|Start your own business]]. If you don't want to work at a firm and already have some experience under your belt, you can start your own business. Home inspection businesses don't have a lot of need for human capital if you're the only one that will inspect the homes. To start your own home inspection company, you'll need a reliable vehicle, a computer and a minimum of $25,000 in working capital for overhead items.
#*Consider incorporating your business to protect yourself from bankruptcy if your company fails.
#*A large initial cost that you'll have to invest in is business insurance.
#*Other potential costs include marketing and advertising, tools, association dues, and office space.

#Purchase a home inspecting franchise. A home inspection franchise will give you the initial tools and contacts that are required to land clients and start making money. Marketing and advertising is also usually covered in the form of logos and other promotional materials. Also, they will have methods that have been proven to be profitable in the past, as well as additional support if you're unsure what to do as a business owner. While the cost of a franchise can sometimes be costly, it may be worth the cost if you have limited experience.

#*Initial costs, including an intial franchise fee can cost anywhere up to $40,000 and more.<ref>https://winfranchising.com/learn-about-win/what-are-my-startup-costs/</ref>[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 7.jpg|center]]
#*Remember to read the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) before purchasing any franchise.
#*Popular home inspection franchises that you can purchase include Ameri-Spec Inspection Services, Home Team, WIN, and A Pro.
===Honing Your Skills==

#Join a home inspectors organization. A home inspectors group will provide you a wealth of knowledge in the form of distance education and classroom training. The top organizations for home inspectors include the NAHI (The National Association of Home Inspectors) and the ASHI (The American Society of Home Inspectors). Both of these organizations have a significant number of members who work professionally as home inspectors. In addition to the education, you'll also be able to attend chapter meetings and workshops to talk about inspection and regulation.<ref>http://www.homeinspector.org/Become-a-home-inspector</ref>

#Get a mentor when first starting off. Some states require you dedicate hours towards an apprenticeship before you can become a certified home inspector. Even if your state doesn't require this, shadowing and working under a seasoned home inspector will give you insight and skills on how you should inspect homes. If you're part of a home inspector association, talk to veteran inspectors and ask if you can be an apprentice under them. If you aren't in an organization contact different firms and see if there is anyone available to take you under their wing.<ref>http://www.jobmonkey.com/howto/home-inspector/</ref>
#*Being an apprentice will also give you hands-on training.

#*You can ask by saying something like, "I really respect the great work you do and all your experience. I'm looking for someone who could guide me and show me the ropes. Do you think I could work with you for a little bit?"

#Go for additional training and education once you're an inspector. Look for regional meetings and seminars that you can attend to stay current and accurate. Many chapters of home inspection organizations will often put on educational events and workshops for existing inspectors.<ref>http://www.homeinspector.org/Calendar</ref> Also, you can use the time around your peers to network with other inspectors.
#*Follow up with people that you meet at educational workshops and training by calling them on the phone or shooting them an email.

#*In some states, like Oregon, you have to complete some continuing education classes to keep your home inspection license up to date.<ref>https://www.oregon.gov/CCB/licensing/Pages/homeinspectorce.aspx</ref>

== Steps ==
===  Education and Training ===

# Take some classes in home inspections. Even if you have experience in construction, plumbing or electric work, a course in home inspections will help you focus on what inspectors must look for.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 1.jpg|center]]
#* Look for online learning opportunities. Many training programs can be found through national educators such as Kaplan, ITT or AHIT.
#* Check with your local community college. You can find instruction for new home inspectors as well as experienced inspectors in local classrooms.
# Work with the American Society of Home Inspectors (ASHI). This organization offers its members ongoing training and educational opportunities.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 2.jpg|center]]
# Find ways to get hands-on experience. Accompany a home inspector to a property and watch how he or she works. Ask questions and take notes.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 3.jpg|center]]
===  Testing and Certification ===
# Check the regulations in your state. Each state has its own set of guidelines and requirements for home inspectors.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 4.jpg|center]]
#* Contact your state's licensing board for information on what kind of certification, if any, is required. You can also utilize ASHI, which often has state and local chapters to help.

# Register for any required testing. Even if your state does not require testing and certification, it is a good idea to take and pass a national home inspector test. It will add to your credibility when looking for work.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 5.jpg|center]]

#* Take the National Home Inspector Board Exam, administered by the Examination Board of Professional Home Inspectors. This 4 hour exam consists of 200 question and you are graded on a scale of 200 to 800. A passing score is 500. It will cost around $225 to take this test.

#* Take the Online Inspector Exam, which is free and takes only about an hour to complete. There are 100 questions, and you can earn a score of 0 to 100. A passing score is 80. This test is administered by the International Association of Certified Home Inspectors.

# Look for as many certification opportunities as you can find. Your state might require you to pass an exam and earn a certification. You can also be certified by organizations such as ASHI and the National Association of Home Inspectors (NAHI).[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 6.jpg|center]]

# Pay any fees associated with certification. Some states will not require certification, but will expect you to pay for a license to do home inspections.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 7.jpg|center]]
===  Finding Work ===
# Join a company. You can look for property inspection companies that may be hiring or inquire about opportunities with existing businesses.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 8.jpg|center]]

# Start your own business. You can work on a contract or freelance basis on your own, or get together with some other inspectors to start a home inspection business.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 9.jpg|center]]

# Market yourself. Promote your experience, training, certifications and other abilities, such as low prices, fast turnaround and immediate appointments.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 10.jpg|center]]

# Utilize your membership in ASHI and other groups to conduct marketing and networking. National and local organizations can help you find opportunities and build your brand.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 11.jpg|center]]

# Develop good relationships with real estate agents. Their clients will often look for referrals when it comes to getting an inspection, and real estate agents can provide your name.[[Image:Become a Home Inspector Step 12.jpg|center]]
== Tips ==

* Continue your education. Many property inspectors take classes and stay current in their field so they can grow their businesses or diversify into other areas, such as construction or building inspections.

# Join a company. You can look for property inspection companies that may be hiring or inquire about opportunities with existing businesses.
# Start your own business. You can work on a contract or freelance basis on your own, or get together with some other inspectors to start a home inspection business.
# Market yourself. Promote your experience, training, certifications and other abilities, such as low prices, fast turnaround and immediate appointments.
# Utilize your membership in ASHI and other groups to conduct marketing and networking. National and local organizations can help you find opportunities and build your brand.
# Develop good relationships with real estate agents. Their clients will often look for referrals when it comes to getting an inspection, and real estate agents can provide your name.
== Tips ==

* Continue your education. Many property inspectors take classes and stay current in their field so they can grow their businesses or diversify into other areas, such as construction or building inspections.
